stories.title: John McCullough of Kennedy Wilson Multifamily Development: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Since joining Kennedy Wilson following the firm’s $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers’ apartment living platform in 2025, John McCullough has been serving as president of the real estate investment company’s multifamily development group, where he oversees every aspect of the firm’s U.S. development business. Kennedy Wilson’s acquisition of Toll Brothers’ platform gave it general partner interests in 18 apartment and student housing properties, with assets under management of $2.2 billion. The firm also purchased a pipeline of 29 development sites in various stages of construction. Toll Brothers’ entire apartment living management team has transitioned over to Kennedy Wilson under the leadership of McCullough, who previously led apartment living operations at Toll Brothers. But McCullough’s real estate path wasn’t always laid out for him, as he started out in the U.S. Navy and then eventually hit his business stride at school in Boston. Commercial Observer caught up with McCullough last month to discuss his entry into real estate, the Toll Brothers acquisition, and his mission at Kennedy Wilson. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: How’d you get started in real estate? John McCullough: I got started in real estate in a roundabout way. I went to the United States Naval Academy for my undergrad, and graduated in 1994, and then served five years in what we would refer to as the surface navy. If I had stayed in the Navy long-term, I would have trained to be the captain of a ship. I served on two large aircraft carriers out in San Diego, and it was a great experience. It was a really good grounding in the fundamentals of leadership I was put into a lot of situations that were incredibly difficult as a 23- or 24-year-old, but I learned a lot from that. bullets: Kennedy Wilson acquired Toll Brothers apartment platform for $347M in 2025.
Deal includes 18 operating properties ($2.2B AUM) and 29 development sites in pipeline.
John McCullough leads multifamily development group post-acquisition.
stories.summary: Kennedy Wilson closed a $347 million acquisition of Toll Brothers' apartment living platform in 2025, gaining control of 18 operating apartment and student housing properties with $2.2 billion in assets under management, plus a pipeline of 29 development sites at various construction stages. John McCullough, former head of apartment operations at Toll Brothers, now leads Kennedy Wilson's multifamily development group with the entire management team transitioning over. This consolidation expands Kennedy Wilson's development scale and land pipeline significantly.
stories.impact: Major platform acquisition signals capital aggregation and operational consolidation in multifamily development. Kennedy Wilson's 29-site pipeline and management bench strengthen its ability to move faster on land plays and construction in key markets; watch for accelerated starts and land acquisition announcements from the combined entity in 2026–2027, particularly in Toll Brothers' legacy markets.

stories.title: Southern Land Company Hires Tony Marchbanks as Head of Homebuilding
stories.excerpt: Southern Land Company has made a leadership hire to spearhead single-family home development in three key states, Commercial Observer has learned. Tony Marchbanks has joined the firm as national president of homebuilding, in which he will focus not only on the U.S., but also focus particularly on Tennessee, Texas and Colorado, according to Southern Land. Marchbanks brings with him 30 years of real estate experience and most recently served as chief operating officer for Highland Homes, where he launched a building spree in the Houston market, producing 1,000 homes per year, Southern Land said. “Higher interest rates and lack of job growth all culminate into a lack of consumer confidence, so you have all three key contributors to a good homebuilding environment that are headwinds at this time,” Marchbanks told CO. “But for a company like Southern Land, it’s actually a huge opportunity because they have expansion plans, particularly into Texas, which is the largest new home market in the country,” Marchbanks said. “Most builders secured their lot supply three years ago, and now they have too many lots. So it’s an opportunity for a company like Southern Land to find and [invest] in communities they wouldn’t have been able to in a strong market.” Southern Land is currently developing four master-planned communities across 5,000 individual lots in its portfolio. Marchbanks will oversee the construction, purchasing, sales and architecture for those soon-to-be neighborhoods. Southern Land has been making some changes in recent months by launching its own mortgage lending division in May to augment its sales division and support its construction pipeline, CO reported at the time. Build-to-sell homes are not the only residential asset class Southern Land has been dabbling in either, as it builds multifamily properties in Las Vegas; Erie, Colo.; and just outside Austin, Tex. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Southern Land hires Tony Marchbanks (ex-Highland Homes COO) as national homebuilding president.
Marchbanks launched 1,000 homes/year production in Houston; targets Tennessee, Texas, Colorado.
Competitor lot oversupply creates acquisition opportunity for well-capitalized builders.
stories.summary: Southern Land Company hired Tony Marchbanks, former COO of Highland Homes where he scaled production to 1,000 homes annually in Houston, as national president of homebuilding. Marchbanks will focus expansion into Tennessee, Texas, and Colorado—markets where most builders are lot-constrained after securing inventory three years ago. He noted that higher rates and weak job growth are headwinds for the sector but represent a consolidation opportunity for well-capitalized firms.
stories.impact: Lot market distress in single-family signals broader capital availability gap; builders with dry powder are positioning to acquire underutilized inventories at discounts. Texas supply tightening (largest new-home market) could redirect some demand into rental housing, particularly in Austin, Dallas, and Houston submarkets where multifamily absorbs overflow demand during affordability crises. Watch for Southern Land to stabilize lot costs, lowering relative advantage of renting vs. buying and tempering near-term multifamily leasing upside in those metros.

stories.title: How Trent Johnson, Brian Landrum at Harbert Management Corp. Invest in Senior Housing
stories.excerpt: Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum are senior managing directors and co-heads of the seniors housing team at Harbert Management Corporation, an $8 billion alternatives asset management firm founded in 1993. The group has been investing in the seniors housing space for 15 years, raising a $210 million investment fund in 2016 and a $510 million investment fund for the space in 2020. The group is currently on its third fundraise, as they attempt to capitalize on the first wave of Baby Boomers turning 80-years-old in 2016. The duo sat down with Commercial Observer to discuss their careers, how the asset class has evolved, the present and future of the senior housing space, and where the best investment opportunities will be in an increasingly important asset class. (This conversation has been edited for length and clarity) Commercial Observer: How long have you been involved in the senior housing space? Trent Johnson: I started investing in the space in 2012, which is where I met Brian at Fortress Investment Group. I actually came from a legal background. I started out as a real estate lawyer, and then I spent a lot of years at an apartment investment and management company, which was a large multifamily REIT based out of Denver, Colo, Apartment Investment and Management Company. I was recruited away to start and lead a seniors housing platform in Dallas, which is where I joined forces with Brian, and we co-headed that office here in Dallas. Brian Landrum: I started investing in seniors housing in 2009 at a predecessor firm, Walton Street Capital, which was a diversified real estate private equity firm, and then in 2012, I joined forces with Trent in 2012 at Fortress Investment Group, which is where we began working together, and then ultimately, made a decision to join up at Harbert Management Corporation in 2015. bullets: Harbert Management raising third seniors housing fund; prior funds: $210M (2016), $510M (2020).
Demographic tailwind: first wave Baby Boomers turned 80 in 2016; acceleration expected.
15-year track record investing in seniors housing as dedicated asset class.
stories.summary: Harbert Management, an $8 billion alternatives firm, is on its third fundraise for seniors housing after raising $210 million in 2016 and $510 million in 2020. Senior managing directors Trent Johnson and Brian Landrum, who have invested in the space since 2012, are capitalizing on Baby Boomers turning 80 (first wave hit in 2016) and expect accelerating demand in the coming decade. The firm has deployed across 15 years of market cycles and specializes in the asset class.
stories.impact: Seniors housing capital is flowing and demographic demand is crystallizing; this creates a parallel, non-competing demand stream but signals institutional capital flight from traditional multifamily into higher-barrier, slower-turnover assets. Expect continued bifurcation of institutional capital—stability-focused seniors/healthcare vs. multifamily yield-chase. For multifamily developers, this means tighter debt markets for standard housing (seniors funds not competing for standard apartments) but also a reminder that demographic optionality (conversion to senior housing, licensed beds) can add value to land and stabilized assets.

stories.title: Sunday Summary: The Rent is Too Damn Low!
stories.excerpt: Back in 2010, Jimmy McMillan ran for governor of New York on a pretty straightforward platform: The rent was too damn high. McMillan said it again and again, and named his political party The Rent is Too Damn High Party. (McMillan’s presence on the debate stage garnered national attention and Matthew Yglesias even titled a slim book with the same name.) Sixteen years later, McMillan is still not wrong, in that the average monthly rent just hit $6,655 in Manhattan according to research from Corcoran Sunshine — which is 10 percent higher than it was a year ago. There are a number of solutions that the Mamdani administration have proffered, but one that has perhaps attracted the most attention has been freezing rents on rent-stabilized apartments. In June, the Rent Guidelines Board issued a freeze on one- and two-year leases, which will certainly be popular with rent-stabilized voters. But one has to wonder if it will actually address the larger issue of affordability — especially if landlords begin to lose more money than they make on stabilized units. Some landlords are keeping units off the market rather than getting them in rentable shape. “Some of [the rent-stabilized units] require more work than others, but for the ones that need significant work — and I mean baseline, just to get them up to livable standards — we’re talking $30,000 minimum,” said Jose Tur, who owns two stabilized buildings in Washington Heights and testified before the RGB before their vote. In addition to the baseline, Tur told Commercial Observer that he would probably have to include another $30,000 per unit for the cosmetic fixes. And that’s on the lower end of the renovation spectrum. Matthew Engel, president of Langsam Property Services, says he has units that require $80,000 to $100,000 worth of work, and rent as low as $600 per month. “There’s no way for me to finance that work,” said Engel. “No bank would lend me $100,000 if I’m only going to be able to collect $6,000 a year in rent.”
bullets: Manhattan average rent hit $6,655/month; up 10% YoY per Corcoran Sunshine.
NYC Rent Guidelines Board froze rents on rent-stabilized leases in June 2025.
Landlords risk keeping stabilized units off-market if losses exceed returns.
stories.summary: Manhattan rents reached $6,655 per month on average, a 10 percent year-over-year increase, according to Corcoran Sunshine research. The Mamdani administration's Rent Guidelines Board froze rents on one- and two-year rent-stabilized leases in June to address affordability. The article cautions that rent freezes may backfire if landlords withdraw stabilized units from the rental market to avoid operating losses.
stories.impact: Rent freezes reduce effective supply of stabilized inventory and push stabilized-unit holders to convert or demolish rather than rent below cost. This concentrates luxury and market-rate supply in Manhattan, raising competition for new construction absorption and pushing developers toward higher-ASP products. Watch for accelerated decontrol/buyout activity in NYC as stabilized buildings become value destructive; this compresses the already-tight Manhattan multifamily pipeline and supports pricing for new Class A product in 2026–2027.

stories.title: AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South
stories.excerpt: A new lease with AI-native fund administrator Hanover Park and the expansion and extension of PMG Worldwide’s existing space have been recent highlights at TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Ave. South, which has seen more than 100,000 square feet of leasing activity in the past year. The recent transactions follow K Health’s long-term renewal and the expansion of another TAMI user completed in late 2025. Hanover Park signed a lease for the building’s entire 10th floor, totaling approximately 19,269 square feet. PMG Worldwide renewed its lease on the entire second floor while expanding into the entire third floor, bringing its total footprint to approximately 38,744 square feet. “We’re pleased to welcome Hanover Park to 387 Park Avenue South and to expand our relationship with PMG Worldwide,” said Joe Lanzilotta, Director, Commercial Asset Management at TF Cornerstone. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” The post AI-Native Hanover Park Leases Full Floor at 387 Park Ave. South appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hanover Park (AI-native fund admin) leases full 10th floor; 19,269 SF at 387 Park Ave South.
PMG Worldwide expands and renews 2nd/3rd floors (38,744 SF total) same building.
Property achieved 100,000+ SF leasing activity in past year; strong TAMI user demand.
stories.summary: TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South in Manhattan saw Hanover Park, an AI-native fund administrator, lease the entire 10th floor (19,269 SF), and PMG Worldwide expand and renew for a combined 38,744 SF footprint. The property has executed over 100,000 SF of leasing in the past year and continues to attract TAMI (tech, media, advertising, information services) and life sciences tenants.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; office leasing vigor in Manhattan signals continued worker footfall and demand for residential proximity to tech hubs. However, the strong TAMI leasing at this midtown address underscores that not all office is weak; specialized, high-barrier sectors (AI, fintech) are consolidating and expanding in prime locations, supporting residential demand from high-earner cohorts in adjacent Hudson Yards and Midtown West multifamily corridors.

stories.title: PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital
stories.excerpt: PMB, a leading healthcare real estate developer, and Loma Linda University Health with Lifepoint Rehabilitation, a business unit of Lifepoint Health, recently broke ground on a new, 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Redlands. Located at 11207 New Jersey., the three-story facility will function as a standalone hospital. “Breaking ground today represents far more than just laying the foundation for a new building – it’s a promise to the community,” said Nolan Weinberg, SVP of Development for PMB. “Inpatient rehabilitation is a critical bridge between acute medical recovery and returning to everyday life..” Loma Linda University Rehabilitation Hospital will be jointly operated by Loma Linda University Health and Lifepoint Rehabilitation. A summer 2028 opening is expected. Upon completion, Loma Linda University Health will transition its existing inpatient rehabilitation unit to the new facility. PMB’s partners on the project include general contractor Layton Construction, architect Material Design Architects and financing partner Harrison Street Asset Management. The post PMB, Loma Linda University Health Break Ground on Inpatient Rehab Hospital appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: PMB and Loma Linda University Health break ground on 99,000 SF, 80-bed inpatient rehab hospital.
Location: Redlands, CA (11207 New Jersey St.); opens summer 2028.
Partners: Layton Construction, Material Design Architects, Harrison Street financing.
stories.summary: PMB and Loma Linda University Health, in partnership with Lifepoint Rehabilitation, broke ground on a 99,000-square-foot, 80-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Redlands, California. The three-story standalone facility, financed by Harrison Street Asset Management, is expected to open in summer 2028. Upon completion, Loma Linda will transition its existing inpatient rehab unit to the new facility.
stories.impact: Healthcare real estate and multifamily are tangential; however, 80-bed inpatient hospital in Inland Empire/Redlands area signals healthcare infrastructure build-out supporting broader population growth in the region. Inpatient rehab facilities typically attract visiting family and recovery-phase temporary housing, indirectly supporting short-term rental demand and operational multifamily in peripheral metros like San Bernardino County.

stories.title: Astoria Favorite :3Coffee Roasters Expands to Halletts Point
stories.excerpt: The Durst Organization has signed :3Coffee Roasters to a 1,232-square-foot lease for a new retail location at 30 Halletts Point in Astoria, Queens. Expected to open later this year, the new shop marks an expansion for the family-owned business and its second Astoria location. It will also be the first retail at 20 and 30 Halletts Point, which opened last year with 647 apartments. “Halletts Point is a thriving community with spectacular views of Manhattan and Queens. As the neighborhood continues to grow, we are selecting retailers that will bring additional value to residents and neighbors alike, and we are excited to welcome :3Coffee Roasters,” said Jody Durst, president of The Durst Organization. :3Coffee Roasters was founded by Astoria residents Fabian Guzman and Andrea Gomez. The brand first opened on Steinway Street in Astoria and later expanded to the Flatiron District in Manhattan, building a following for their neighborhood-oriented approach and high-quality offerings. The Durst Organization was represented in-house by Karen Rose and Eric Engelhardt and by KSR’s Zach Nathan, Mark Gallucci, and Hunter Lazan. :3Coffee Roasters was represented by Genaro Otero at Sinvin. The post Astoria Favorite :3Coffee Roasters Expands to Halletts Point appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: :3Coffee Roasters signs 1,232 SF retail lease at 30 Halletts Point, Astoria, Queens.
30 Halletts Point opened last year with 647 apartments; first retail activation.
Second Astoria location for coffee roaster; neighborhood-focused operator.
stories.summary: The Durst Organization leased 1,232 SF at 30 Halletts Point in Astoria, Queens to :3Coffee Roasters, a family-owned coffee brand founded by Astoria residents. The lease marks the first retail activation at the 647-unit apartment building that opened in 2025 and is the coffee roaster's second location in the neighborhood. Durst is actively curating retail tenants to anchor the mixed-use community.
stories.impact: Direct positive signal for residential mixed-use in Astoria: a 647-unit building achieving retail activation one year after opening confirms demand-side tenant interest and suggests Durst is successfully curating street-level experience to drive resident and visitor traffic. This validates Halletts Point pricing and leasing velocity and suggests Astoria waterfront (Long Island City submarket extension) continues to absorb new multifamily with strong co-tenancy. Early retail success de-risks future development in the corridor and supports acquisition values for resi-centric sites.

stories.title: CBRE Arranges Debt on Advanced Manufacturing Campus in San Jose’s Golden Triangle
stories.excerpt: CBRE announced it arranged $67.4 million in financing for Forge North First, a mixed-phase industrial/R&D campus and advanced manufacturing development in San Jose’s Golden Triangle submarket. Mike Walker, Brad Zampa and Andy Gross of CBRE’s Debt & Structured Finance team in San Francisco arranged the five-year bridge loan with floating-rate, non-recourse financing from an institutional lender on behalf of Four Corners Properties and a West Coast-based institutional investor. “The combination of surging occupier demand and extremely limited supply positions Four Corners to create significant value at Forge North First,” said Zampa. Four Corners, an established local investor and developer founded in 2005, has invested in 50 buildings totaling 7.2 million square feet. In January 2026, Four Corners and its institutional partner acquired the existing 205,800-square-foot, five-building campus from BXP. The mixed-phase program includes comprehensive modernization of the existing campus and development of two advanced manufacturing buildings totaling approximately 239,000 square feet. bullets: CBRE arranged $67.4M bridge loan for Forge North First advanced manufacturing campus, San Jose.
Four Corners Properties + institutional partner acquired 205,800 SF campus from BXP in Jan 2026.
Development adds 239,000 SF of advanced manufacturing buildings; modernization of existing structures.
stories.summary: CBRE's Debt & Structured Finance team in San Francisco arranged a $67.4 million, five-year floating-rate bridge loan for Forge North First, an industrial/R&D and advanced manufacturing campus in San Jose's Golden Triangle submarket. Four Corners Properties and an institutional investor acquired the existing 205,800-square-foot, five-building campus from BXP in January 2026 and plan to modernize it while adding two new advanced manufacturing buildings totaling approximately 239,000 SF.
stories.impact: Surge in advanced manufacturing demand (semiconductors, EV supply chain, nearshoring) is concentrating in San Jose Golden Triangle, driving institutional capital and debt availability for industrial/R&D redevelopment. This capital intensity and land scarcity in Bay Area tech hubs will continue to compress residential land availability and elevate multifamily construction costs through labor and materials competition. Four Corners' aggressive capital deployment signals bullish view on West Coast advanced manufacturing durability; multifamily developers competing for labor and land in Silicon Valley should expect continued headwinds through 2027–2028.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap Closes Sale of Downtown Westfield Mixed-Use
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap arranged the sale of 251 North Ave. W., a mixed-use property in Westfield, NJ, for $5,260,000. Alan Cafiero, David Cafiero and Damien Rance of Marcus & Millichap exclusively marketed the property on behalf of the seller and procured the private buyer. “Downtown Westfield continues to be one of the most desirable mixed-use investment markets in New Jersey,” said Alan Cafiero, senior managing director investments in Marcus & Millichap’s New Jersey office. “The combination of a premier downtown location, immediate proximity to the train station and a strong, diverse tenant roster generated significant investor interest in this asset.” The property is a three-story, 17,831-square-foot building on a 0.18-acre lot with direct access to municipal commuter parking. It has nine suites and was renovated in 2014. The rent roll features a diverse mix of service-oriented tenants, including Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, the State of New Jersey, BAYADA Home Health Care and Rooster Spin. The post Marcus & Millichap Closes Sale of Downtown Westfield Mixed-Use appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap closed $5.26M sale of 251 North Ave., Westfield, NJ mixed-use.
Three-story, 17,831 SF building; nine suites; diverse tenant mix (Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, BAYADA).
Location: immediate proximity to commuter rail; renovated 2014.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap brokered the $5.26 million sale of a three-story, 17,831-square-foot mixed-use property at 251 North Avenue West in downtown Westfield, New Jersey. The nine-suite building features diverse service-oriented tenants including Columbia Bank, Edward Jones, and BAYADA Home Health Care, and benefits from direct access to municipal parking and proximity to commuter rail. The property was renovated in 2014.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; however, Westfield's positioning as a 'most desirable mixed-use investment market' in NJ signals suburban tertiary-market appetite and transit-oriented value capture. Strong commuter rail access and diverse service tenants support demand for nearby rental housing from working professionals; this validates residential development interest in connected suburban NJ corridors and suggests rental demand durability in commuter-shed markets serving NYC.

stories.title: Nuveen Green Capital Closes $281M Record C-PACE Loan for Boston Condos
stories.excerpt: The steady climb of commercial property assessed clean energy (C-PACE) financing around the U.S. has made its way to one of Boston’s tallest buildings. Millennium Partners has secured a $281 million C-PACE loan to implement energy efficiency upgrades at the 62-story Winthrop Center in Downtown Boston, the developer announced Friday afternoon. Nuveen Green Capital originated the fixed-rate loan under the Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) Massachusetts program which marked the largest C-PACE financing to date in the New England region, according to the lender. The condo inventory of the roughly 800,000 square-foot mixed-use building completed in 2023 attracted strong lender competition with many debt funds chasing the loan, according to a source familiar with the transaction. The C-PACE debt closed concurrently with a $575 million commercial mortgage backed securities (CMBS) loan led by Morgan Stanley for the office and retail portion of the tower according to a presale report from Moody’s. CoStar first reported the MP Trust 2026-WTRP single-asset-single-borrower deal for Boston’s largest building in the city’s financial district. The combined $856 million debt package takes out a prior construction loan from Cale Street in October 2020 after the London firm stepped in following another bank who backed out during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, according to sources. “We were honored to partner with MassDevelopment to recapitalize the largest C-PACE-financed project in New England, one that has helped reshape downtown Boston with state-of-the-art, energy-efficient residences,” Mike Doty, senior director of originations for NGC, said in a statement. Christopher Jeffries, founder of Millennium Partners, said in a statement that the C-PACE loan “recognizes the investments we have made in energy efficiency while providing long-term capital that supports the building’s enduring performance.” The PACE Massachusetts program was updated in June 2026
bullets: Nuveen Green Capital closed $281M C-PACE loan for Millennium Partners' Winthrop Center, Boston.
62-story mixed-use building (800,000 SF, completed 2023); largest C-PACE in New England.
Concurrent $575M CMBS loan led by Morgan Stanley for office component.
stories.summary: Nuveen Green Capital closed a record-breaking $281 million fixed-rate C-PACE (Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy) loan for Millennium Partners' Winthrop Center, a 62-story, 800,000-square-foot mixed-use building in Downtown Boston completed in 2023. The financing, originated under Massachusetts' PACE program and the largest C-PACE ever in New England, was secured concurrently with a $575 million CMBS loan led by Morgan Stanley. Strong lender competition for the condo inventory drove robust debt terms.
stories.impact: C-PACE capital availability is expanding and de-risking retrofit execution for stabilized mixed-use; the $281M facility signals institutional confidence in energy-upgrade financing and suggests developers can more easily layer green financing on top of traditional debt structures. For multifamily developers, this opens alternative leverage routes for efficiency upgrades and repositioning on existing assets, particularly in Northeast markets with mature PACE programs. Watch for increased use of C-PACE to unlock equity from stabilized portfolios without rate cap stress; this may accelerate redeployment into new development and land in 2026–2027.
